method: Read-only hand execution and symbolic tracing of package/artifacts/merge.py against package/task.json, per examiner-charge.md but re-derived from scratch. Unlike the worker (author of the provisional answer), I performed an independent structural enumeration of the domain's boundary classes with fresh witnesses distinct from the worker's [[0,1],[1,2]], plus a loop-invariant argument bounding what overlaps are reachable in merge's output. Components checked: (1) claim reading — task.json forbids i.end >= j.start, so touching output intervals count as violations: PASS. Invariant check: an interval is appended only when s >= out[-1][1], and merges mutate only out[-1], so once a successor is appended the predecessor's end is frozen; every consecutive output pair therefore satisfies i.end <= j.start — strict overlap (>) is unreachable, only equality is, so under a strict-overlap reading the verdict would flip to HOLDS, but the claim as stated uses >=. (2) domain membership of [[0,1],[1,2]] — 2 <= 6 intervals, endpoints in [-10,10], start <= end for each: PASS. (3) mechanical trace — sorted input [[0,1],[1,2]]; out=[[0,1]]; line-8 test 1 < 1 is False; [1,2] appended; returned [[0,1],[1,2]] is already sorted; pair ([0,1],[1,2]) has 1 >= 1: PASS. Independent class search (E-B): touching pair with negative endpoints [[-5,-3],[-3,0]] -> -3 < -3 False -> output [[-5,-3],[-3,0]], -3 >= -3, VIOLATING; zero-width duplicated [[3,3],[3,3]] -> 3 < 3 False -> VIOLATING; zero-width touching a wider interval at its start [[0,0],[0,5]] -> 0 < 0 False -> VIOLATING; at its end [[0,5],[5,5]] -> 5 < 5 False -> VIOLATING; zero-width strictly inside [[0,5],[2,2]] -> 2 < 5 True -> merged [[0,5]], holds; nested [[0,10],[2,5]] -> merged, max keeps 10, holds; positive-width duplicates [[1,4],[1,4]] -> 1 < 4 True -> merged, holds; proper overlap [[0,3],[2,5]] -> merged [[0,5]], holds; empty -> [] (line-3 guard), vacuous; singleton -> loop never runs, vacuous; unsorted [[1,2],[0,1]] -> line 5 sorts, reduces to touching case, VIOLATING. Independent verdict: VIOLATED; the worker's witness is in-domain and mechanically violating; result.json should stand unchanged.

per_distinction.why: My own control-flow analysis of merge.py agrees that the claim's truth turns exactly on where line 8's strict '<' differs from '<=': touching intervals (prev.end == next.start) and zero-width intervals sharing a boundary point. My independent enumeration of the remaining classes (empty, singleton, proper overlap, nested, positive-width duplicates, unsorted order, negative endpoints) matches the worker's: each holds vacuously, merges correctly, or reduces to the turning classes. One refinement that does not change the analysis: a zero-width interval strictly inside a wider interval ([[0,5],[2,2]]) is merged and holds — only zero-width intervals sharing a boundary point violate, which is how the worker scoped that class.

My independent trace of [[0,1],[1,2]] through the actual code text reproduces the worker's: sort leaves it unchanged, out=[[0,1]], the line-8 test 1 < 1 is False, [1,2] is appended, and the sorted output [[0,1],[1,2]] contains i=[0,1] before j=[1,2] with i.end = 1 >= 1 = j.start. The input is in-domain. Verdict VIOLATED is correct, and I additionally verified via the loop invariant that no strict overlap (i.end > j.start) is reachable — so the violation genuinely hinges on the '>=' in the claim, exactly as the worker's mechanism states.
